blocks.text: — — — bury the slaughtered bulls. (A thing known by experience) from the rotting flesh everywhere flower-gathering bees are born, which, after the manner of their parents, tend the fields, are devoted to their work, and labor in hope.
But most fully of all, the prince of poets, in the fourth book of the Georgics [vs. 554 ff.], from which it will suffice to have quoted these few lines:

Here indeed they behold a sudden portent, wondrous to tell: through the dissolved flesh of the oxen, throughout the whole belly, bees buzzing, and swarming out of the burst ribs, and vast clouds trailing, and now at the treetop flowing together, and letting down a cluster from the pliant boughs. [III, 355] Since the ancients report these things about the origin of bees with such agreement, it may seem surprising that we read, in Judges, chapter 14, verse 8, that Samson found עדת דברים, a swarm of bees, in the carcass of the lion. All the more so, since bees are said to abstain from flesh and to flee strong smells altogether. Aristotle, book 9, chapter 40: πρὸς σάρκα δὲ οὐδενὸς καθίζει, οὐδὲ ὀψοφαγεῖ [pros sarka de oudenos kathizei, oude opsophagei]; It settles on the flesh of no [col. 504] animal, nor does it crave cooked dishes. Varro, On Agriculture, book 3, chapter 16: None of them settles on a filthy place, or on one that smells bad. Likewise: They do not lick things as flies do, for no one sees them (as one sees flies) on flesh, or blood, or fat. Pliny, book 11, chapter 21, on wasps and hornets: All feed on flesh, unlike bees, which touch no body. Philes on the bee, chapter 28:
Καὶ ζῇ μὲν ἁγνὸν ἡ σοφὴ σχεδὸν βίον, Ἄγευστος οὖσα νεκρικῶν σπαραγμάτων· [Kai zē men hagnon hē sophē schedon bion, Ageustos ousa nekrikōn sparagmatōn]

And the wise creature leads a chaste life, and does not taste the torn flesh of carcasses. Didymus, Geoponica, book 15 [ch. 2, §. 22]: Ἔστι δὲ καὶ καθαρὸν ὑπερβολῇ τὸ ζῶον, οὐδενὶ τῶν δυσωδῶν καὶ ἀκαθάρτων προσιζάνον, οὔτε λίχνον· οὔτε γὰρ σαρξὶν, οὔτε αἵματι, οὔτε λιπάσματι οὐδενὶ προΐπταται· [Esti de kai katharon hyperbolē to zōon, oudeni tōn dysōdōn kai akathartōn prosizanon, oute lichnon; oute gar sarxin, oute haimati, oute lipasmati oudeni proiptatai] It is also an exceedingly clean animal, settling on nothing foul-smelling or impure, nor greedy (in Greek οὔτε λίχνον [oute lichnon], which others absurdly render nor to the lamp) for it flies neither to flesh, nor to blood, nor to any fat ^{(2)}. Indeed, if any bee dies in the hive, the survivors carry the carcass out, lest it give off a foul smell. Virgil:
— — — then the bodies of those bereft of light they carry out of the dwellings, and lead mournful funerals.
